questions.question: Which responsibility belongs primarily to a Jenkins controller?
options: Compiling every repository on its local filesystem
Scheduling pipeline work and coordinating agents
Providing one CPU core for every executor
Replacing the external artifact repository
questions.explanation: The controller is the control plane: it serves Jenkins, evaluates and records pipeline state, and schedules work. Build commands should run on agents rather than the built-in node.

questions.question: A team starts 24 builds per hour, and each build consumes 15 executor-minutes on average. What steady executor demand does the model use?
options: 39 executor-minutes per hour
160 executor-minutes per hour
360 executor-minutes per hour
1,440 executor-minutes per hour
questions.explanation: Multiply arrivals by aggregate executor time: 24 builds/hour x 15 executor-minutes/build = 360 executor-minutes per hour.

questions.question: Eight executors process builds that each consume 15 executor-minutes. During a 30-minute burst, arrivals rise to 60 builds per hour. About how many builds accumulate?
options: 0 builds
8 builds
14 builds
28 builds
questions.explanation: Eight executors provide 480 executor-minutes per hour, or 32 builds per hour at 15 minutes each. The 28-build-per-hour deficit lasts half an hour, so about 14 builds accumulate.

questions.question: Why should production Jenkins controllers normally set built-in-node executors to zero?
options: It makes every agent use zero CPU
It prevents pipeline definitions from using stages
It keeps repository-controlled build code off the controller host
It automatically creates ephemeral agents
questions.explanation: A build on the built-in node has the same controller-filesystem access as the Jenkins process. Zero executors prevents that scheduling path, but administrators must also provide agents.

questions.question: A public pull-request test runs inside withCredentials on a shared agent. What is the key security problem?
options: Jenkins log masking makes the test run more slowly
Repository-controlled code can use or exfiltrate the credential despite log masking
The credential ID becomes a Java version
The pull request can no longer produce JUnit XML
questions.explanation: Masking reduces accidental log exposure; it is not a sandbox. Untrusted code must not receive trusted credentials, and secret-bearing jobs should not share an execution boundary with untrusted jobs.

questions.question: What is the intended scope of Jenkins stash and unstash?
options: Long-term promotion across unrelated pipeline runs
Small file transfer between workspaces in one pipeline run
Encrypted backup of the entire controller
Plugin dependency management
questions.explanation: A stash is normally discarded after its pipeline run and is intended for relatively small transfers between that run's nodes. Durable or large release artifacts belong in an external artifact repository.

questions.question: What should a Jenkins upgrade rehearsal preserve and test together?
options: Only the latest Jenkins WAR file
Controller state, plugin versions, configuration, credentials recovery material, and representative pipelines
Only agent workspaces
Only console log colors
questions.explanation: Jenkins behavior is the combination of controller state, core, plugins, configuration, and secrets. A restorable backup and staged rehearsal must exercise that combination before production rollout.
